title: The Electric Seaglider That Flies on a Cushion of Air
summary:
It's a bird! It's a plane! Actually, it's a 50-foot-long electric seaglider. The vessel, built by the MIT alumni-founded company Regent Craft, can float like a boat, rise on hydrofoils, then fly just above the surface at up to 180 miles per hour.

The trick is called the ground effect. Flying close to a surface like water gives an aircraft extra lift and less drag. 'We're flying on a cushion of air just like a bird skimming over the surface,' says Billy Thalheimer, one of the company's founders. The seaglider can travel up to 180 miles on a single charge.

The larger passenger vessel, called Viceroy, has a 65-foot wingspan and first flew this September. It can carry up to 14 people or about 3,500 pounds of cargo. They hope it will combine the speed of planes with the cost of ferries — six times faster than a ferry, Thalheimer says, but half the cost of an airline ticket.

The idea grew from a spectacular flop. In July 2016, Thalheimer and co-founder Mike Klinker entered Red Bull's Flugtag competition, which challenges teams to fly human-powered machines over water. On the bank of Boston's Charles River, they pushed their craft off the edge — and it nosedived into the water. 'The flight went horrendously wrong,' Thalheimer says. 'It was embarrassing, but it was also a really good lesson in engineering and risk mitigation.'

Electric power brings other perks. A jet engine has thousands of complex parts, but Regent's seaglider has a battery with no moving parts and a motor with one moving part. Thalheimer says both vessels have passed their float, foil and fly tests, and the company is 'full speed ahead moving into production.' He imagines trips like New York to the Hamptons — 'like high-speed rail on every coastline of the world.'
why_it_matters: Faster, cheaper trips across water could change how people travel along coasts, and the story shows how a public failure can lead to a better idea.

background_read: A seaglider is a craft that works in three ways: it floats like a boat, rises on hydrofoils, and then flies just above the water.
Flying close to a surface gives an aircraft extra lift and less drag, and this is called the ground effect.
Electric motors have far fewer moving parts than jet engines, which can make them simpler to build and run.
Ferries carry people across water but move slowly, while planes are fast but costly, so a seaglider tries to offer something in between.
